Trump signs executive order to cut childhood vaccines recommendations, drawing medical concern

President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday to reduce the number of vaccines recommended for children, sparking widespread concern among the medical community. The order, which calls for limiting vaccines for other diseases to high-risk populations, still recommends childhood vaccines for 11 diseases, including measles and polio. Trump claimed without evidence that childhood vaccines are linked to an increase in autism diagnoses. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was present for the signing, has maintained this stance as well. The order also advises breaking up the MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella into three separate vaccines. Vaccine advocates and researchers have warned that reducing childhood vaccine recommendations will make children more vulnerable to disease.

Major U.S. medical associations and American doctors were quick to rebuke the executive order as a rejection of science at a time when the United States is experiencing its largest measles resurgence in more than three decades. The National Foundation for Infectious Diseases said in a statement that the nation should be strengthening its ability to protect children, not putting that progress at risk. The American Medical Association criticized the executive order, stating that decisions about how and when vaccines are used should be driven by rigorous scientific evidence, patient safety and independent medical and public health expertise.

Where the accounts differ

UPI reports that the executive order still recommends vaccines for 11 diseases, including measles and polio, while FOX News states that the order recommends vaccines for 11 diseases, fewer than the 18 current CDC guidelines. The Daily Wire and The Guardian both mention that the order reduces the number of diseases from 18 to 11, but The Guardian specifies that only six of the 17 vaccines currently recommended for all children would continue to have full recommendations. CBS News and Axios do not specify the exact number of diseases but both mention the MMR vaccine being split into three separate shots. UPI and The Guardian note that the MMR vaccine is not deadly, while Trump claimed it could be "quite lethal." FOX News and The Daily Wire attribute the claim about the MMR vaccine being "quite lethal" to Trump, while UPI and The Guardian attribute it to Trump as well.

Sources UPI · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News · Axios

Progressive insurgents Francesca Hong and Abdul El-Sayed test Bernie Sanders-style populism in 2026 midterms

Progressive Democrats Francesca Hong and Abdul El-Sayed are running for statewide office in 2026, testing the viability of a leftward shift in the party’s platform. Hong, a state representative in Wisconsin, is leading in the Democratic primary for governor, while El-Sayed, a former public health official, is the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. Both candidates are seen as potential 2028 presidential hopefuls, with their campaigns viewed as experiments in embracing a more radical form of populism. Hong has emphasized affordability and opposed data center construction, while El-Sayed has pushed for Medicare for All and other progressive policies. Their campaigns are closely watched by party leaders who are divided on whether such a leftward turn can succeed in a general election.

Hong’s campaign has faced scrutiny over past social media posts, including calls to “cancel Thanksgiving” and “defund then abolish” the police. She has since walked back these statements, claiming she has “evolved.” El-Sayed, meanwhile, has distanced himself from the “democratic socialist” label, though he has supported policies like abolishing ICE and expanding Medicare. Both candidates are navigating the challenge of balancing progressive ideals with the need to appeal to a broader electorate, particularly as Republicans are actively promoting their campaigns in the general election.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Hong told Politico that a win in November could signal to candidates that working-class issues are a priority. Washington Examiner states that Hong has walked back her 2020 call to “cancel Thanksgiving” and her 2019 and 2021 calls to “defund then abolish” the police. New York Post notes that Hong disavowed her anti-law enforcement positions when confronted with her past statements. The Daily Wire and The Free Press both highlight Hong’s past calls to “defund then abolish” the police and her 2020 tweet about canceling Thanksgiving. Straight Arrow News mentions that Axelrod called Hong “a font of zany liberal, faculty lounge exotica,” while Axios describes her as a “self-described democratic socialist.”

Sources Axios · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Free Press · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Iran threat prompted secret Trump flight from Turkiye: Reports

President Donald Trump secretly switched planes during his departure from Turkey last month, using a catering truck to transfer to a smaller military aircraft, according to multiple U.S. media reports. The maneuver was reportedly triggered by a credible Iranian assassination threat. Trump initially stated he would depart on the older Air Force One, but he was instead moved to a C-32A military jet. The Washington Post and The New York Times reported that the older Air Force One served as a decoy, with journalists and some White House staff unaware of the switch. Trump later appeared on the older aircraft in the UK, though the exact method of his transfer from the C-32A to the Air Force One remains unclear. White House Communications Director Steve Cheung defended the new Air Force One, calling it a state-of-the-art aircraft with high-level security protocols.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and Newsweek both report that Trump was moved via a catering truck to a C-32A aircraft, with the older Air Force One serving as a decoy. However, Newsweek adds that Trump initially stated there was no security concern and that the Qatari-gifted jet had been sent ahead for American service members to tour. CBS News and BBC both mention that the Secret Service advised Trump to take the older plane for security reasons, a detail not included in Al Jazeera or Newsweek. FOX News and BBC note that Trump was seen boarding the older Air Force One in Ankara, but FOX News adds that the legacy jet initially appeared on radar without a call sign before taking the "AF1" call sign midflight, a detail not mentioned in other accounts. The Washington Examiner and CBS News both cite the Washington Post as the source of the report, while BBC and FOX News also reference the Post but add specific details about the operation, such as the involvement of War Secretary Pete Hegseth boarding the C-32A separately.

Sources Al Jazeera · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · FOX News · BBC · CBS News

Timeline: Issues abound after Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovations

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool faced multiple issues following a multi-million dollar renovation. The project, initially promoted by President Donald Trump, led to disputes over the cause of damage to the pool’s surface. Federal prosecutors, led by U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, moved to dismiss a felony charge against former Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of vandalizing the pool. The motion cited evidence that the damage was the result of flawed installation by the contractor. Trump, however, continued to claim that the damage was caused by vandals, despite acknowledging there was "no video or proof" of such acts. The pool also experienced algae blooms and peeling of the new protective coating, prompting National Park Service crews to clean the area and apply hydrogen peroxide to the water.

The renovation, which included repainting the pool’s basin in "American flag blue," was initially estimated to cost $1.5 million to $2 million and take a week. However, the final cost reached $16 million, and the project took months to complete. A lawsuit was filed by the Cultural Landscape Foundation, arguing that the blue paint violated federal law by altering the design intent of the National Mall. The pool was eventually reopened after a series of repairs and adjustments, though issues persisted, including peeling and a tear in the sealant.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News and The Guardian both mention that the Cultural Landscape Foundation filed a lawsuit against the Interior Department, citing the blue paint as a violation of federal law. The Guardian adds that the pool was drained and repainted as part of a beautification push tied to America’s 250th anniversary celebrations. ABC News and The Guardian note that the Justice Department moved to dismiss the case against Hearn, acknowledging the damage was due to a botched installation. FOX News and The Guardian both cite a National Park Service employee as a "highly credible witness" who allegedly saw Hearn "violently" rip and tug at the pool’s coating, though FOX News provides more specific details about the employee’s account and the court documents. Straight Arrow News and ABC News both mention that Hearn denied damaging the pool and claimed he was only checking the liner, but ABC News adds that Hearn’s lawyers described the case as "continued harassment."

Sources Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · FOX News · ABC News · The Guardian · NPR

Wildfires Spread Rapidly in Pacific Northwest and Western Canada

Wildfires are spreading rapidly in the Pacific Northwest and western Canada, with extreme fire behavior reported in several regions. The National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) reported 101 new fires on August 9, including nine large fires, with nearly 30,000 firefighters battling 98 uncontained large fires. The Northwest remains the most active fire region in the U.S., with 46 uncontained large fires burning in Washington and Oregon. In British Columbia, a state of emergency was declared as more than 100 wildfires burned, with the Bald Range fire being labeled "out of control." The fire forced thousands to evacuate, including 12,000 in Summerland and 8,000 in Peachland. A woman died while attempting to flee the fire, according to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

In Oregon, the Wrights Spring Fire has burned 46,769 acres and remains 0% contained, with 555 firefighters assigned to the incident. The fire prompted evacuations and road closures, and a contract dozer operator, Jason Ensign, died while supporting suppression efforts. In Washington, the Little Giant Fire has burned 116,956 acres and destroyed 26 structures, with 1,813 personnel assigned to the incident. The fire is one of several major incidents in the region, with extreme fire behavior reported.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek reports that the Wrights Spring Fire burned 46,769 acres and that Jason Ensign died while operating a bulldozer. NPR states that the Wrights Spring Fire burned 33,000 acres and that Jason Ensign died battling the fire. The Guardian and UPI mention the death of an 80-year-old woman during the Bald Range fire evacuation, while BBC and Straight Arrow News also report the woman's death. The Guardian and BBC note that the Bald Range fire burned 53 sq miles, while UPI states it was 13,618 hectares (approximately 53 sq miles). NPR and UPI both mention the Widemouth 2 fire in Utah, with NPR stating it burned 118,000 acres and UPI confirming the same figure. The Guardian and BBC report that the Bald Range fire was 0% contained, while UPI states it was labeled "out of control."

Sources Newsweek · NPR · The Guardian · UPI · BBC · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Max Miller locked in for reelection bid after Ohio ballot deadline passes

Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) will continue to run for reelection after the 4 p.m. Monday certification deadline passed, despite allegations of domestic violence made against him by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. Miller is now locked in as the Republican nominee, as Ohio law required county party chairs to notice a nominating meeting at least two days in advance. He has denied the allegations, which include claims of scalding Moreno with hot water, holding a gun to her head, and fracturing their daughter’s collarbone. Democrats view the race as increasingly competitive, with Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, as the likely Democratic candidate. Recent polls show Poindexter leading Miller by 8 points, though Trump won the district by 11 points in 2024. Miller has called for a House Ethics Committee investigation into himself.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and ABC News both state that Miller was never criminally charged in connection with the dispute, while The Daily Caller and FOX News mention that Miller accused his ex-wife of fabricating the allegations due to her mental illness. The Washington Examiner and ABC News report that the Department of Children and Family Services did not find evidence to substantiate child abuse allegations, while The Daily Caller and FOX News include specific details about the alleged incidents, such as scalding Moreno with hot water from a skillet and breaking their daughter’s collarbone. The Daily Caller and ABC News note that Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, told police that her daughter received physical injuries while in Miller’s care, which is not mentioned in the Washington Examiner or FOX News accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · NPR · FOX News · ABC News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Scores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of country

A powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, causing widespread damage and resulting in at least 111 deaths. The quake, which occurred at 7:34 a.m. local time, had its epicenter in the western department of Chocó. The US and Colombian geological surveys confirmed the magnitude and location. The president of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, declared a national state of emergency, stating that 111 people had been killed and 87 injured, with 61 buildings collapsed. The hardest-hit cities included Cali, Pereira, and Manizales, where significant damage was reported. Authorities in Cali reported at least 20 buildings collapsed, while Pereira's mayor said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims trapped in at least 15 of them. The earthquake was felt in neighboring countries including Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama.

The earthquake caused extensive damage to infrastructure, with reports of collapsed buildings, damaged hospitals, and disrupted transportation systems. Search-and-rescue operations were underway, with residents and emergency crews working to locate survivors. In Manizales, the mayor warned against returning to damaged buildings and urged people to stay outside due to the risk of aftershocks. Social media videos showed the aftermath, including collapsed buildings and people searching for victims in the rubble.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC report different death tolls, with The Guardian stating 111 deaths and BBC reporting at least 132. The UPI and BBC also differ on the number of collapsed buildings, with UPI citing 86 buildings collapsed and BBC reporting 65 in Pereira. The Guardian and NPR both mention 111 deaths, while UPI and BBC report higher numbers. The Guardian and BBC attribute the death toll to different sources, with The Guardian citing the president's statement and BBC reporting from local authorities. The UPI mentions 132 deaths according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, which is not mentioned in other accounts. The Straight Arrow News reports 70 deaths, which is lower than the other outlets. The Associated Press reports 111 deaths, aligning with The Guardian and NPR, but also mentions over 2,700 people missing, which is not included in other accounts.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · UPI · Straight Arrow News · Associated Press · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Hotel staff's failure to secure room keys led to a woman's assault, exposing systemic vulnerabilities in hospitality safety protocols.

Woman assaulted after Travelodge staff gave room key to her abuser

A woman was assaulted by her domestic abuser after Travelodge staff gave him a key to her room. The woman, who remains anonymous, told the BBC she was staying at a London branch of the hotel in October 2025 to escape her abuser. She said the man, who she described as her abuser, entered the hotel and told reception staff he was the boyfriend of a woman staying there, asking for her room number and floor. He was given a key and directed to her room, where he kicked in the door, assaulted her, and tried to grab her phone. The woman ran downstairs, shaking and crying, and was offered another room in the hotel. Travelodge has acknowledged the incident, stating that their room access security policies were not correctly followed and that they have since made changes to strengthen these policies.

Another woman, Jo from Leeds, told BBC News she was attacked in her Travelodge room in July. She said an unknown man entered her room, and her friend heard him say, “I'm sorry, they gave me this key.” Jo criticized Travelodge’s assurances about safety, saying they were not accurate. Travelodge responded by stating that an investigation found their updated security policies were not followed and that they had retrained staff on current procedures.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the woman was staying at the hotel in London in October 2025 and that the abuser told reception staff his girlfriend was having a seizure. The Guardian also mentions a previous case in Maidenhead in 2022 where a man was sentenced to more than seven years in jail after being given a key to a woman’s room and sexually assaulting her. The BBC does not mention this specific case but includes quotes from Jo, a woman from Leeds, and Andy Smith, a frequent Travelodge guest who claims he was given keys to other people’s rooms. The Guardian attributes the statement about the Maidenhead case to the Travelodge spokesperson, while the BBC attributes it to a BBC News report.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · Travelodge

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Trump’s Iran War Is Going Backward

On Saturday, a senior Iranian national security official issued a set of demands that the US must meet before a key waterway for oil shipping can be reopened. Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called for the US to lift its sanctions and naval blockade on Iran, “completely compensate” Iran for war damages, “unconditionally” release frozen Iranian assets, and end all attacks on Iran’s allies in the region. According to multiple media outlets, the US government did not deliver an immediate response to the demands. Many of them resemble those in the interim ceasefire deal signed by the US and Iran in June. Back then, the Trump administration said that it would only lift sanctions completely if the two countries came to an agreement on Iran’s nuclear development. While there was an initial ceasefire, it did not last. A couple of days later, Iran’s military closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil transit point, stating the US violated their agreement by allowing Israel to continue bombing Lebanon. Combat resumed and even expanded to Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and Straight Arrow News both report that Zolghadr listed the same conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, and compensating Iran for war damages. However, Straight Arrow News adds that Zolghadr also demanded the US end aggression against Iran, Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq, and withdraw its naval and air forces from Iran. The Washington Examiner and New York Post also mention these additional demands, while The Hill and UPI do not. The Hill reports that Vice President Vance said the US is “in the middle of the game” with Iran, while the New York Post and Straight Arrow News attribute this statement to Vance as well. The Washington Examiner and New York Post also note that Trump claimed the negotiations were going “very well” and a deal could be “soon,” a claim not mentioned in Mother Jones or Straight Arrow News.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · New York Post · UPI

Netanyahu Rejects Trump’s Gaza Plan: No Withdrawal Until Hamas Gives Up ‘All Weaponry’

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected President Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that Israel will not withdraw from the territory until Hamas is fully disarmed. Netanyahu emphasized that the Israeli military will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas surrenders all its weapons, including heavy and light arms. He said the two sides are still discussing the matter, with some ideas acceptable and others unacceptable to Israel. Trump had promoted the plan as a historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza, with a phased process involving Israeli withdrawal and the establishment of a new Palestinian administration under U.S. supervision.

The plan, negotiated with Arab mediators in Cairo and overseen by Trump’s Board of Peace, outlined a phased process for Hamas to surrender weapons, disclose tunnel locations, and allow a new Palestinian administration to take control. Israeli forces would leave only after areas were verified as demilitarized. Netanyahu, however, insisted that full disarmament must come first, and Israeli troops would not withdraw beyond current lines until Hamas’s weapons are fully decommissioned. The Israeli military has scaled back attacks since a meeting with the Board of Peace’s representative, Nikolay Mladenov, on Monday.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Netanyahu’s comments were directed at the U.S. and that Israel has continued attacks on Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire. The Daily Wire and UPI mention that Israel has scaled back attacks since meeting with Mladenov, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News include statistics on Palestinian casualties and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant. The Guardian and The Daily Wire note that Netanyahu is facing elections in October, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News include quotes from Hamas officials about expecting the U.S. to pressure Netanyahu. The Daily Wire and The Guardian attribute the characterization of the plan as “genuine disarmament” to Netanyahu, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News attribute it to Netanyahu as well.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · Straight Arrow News · UPI · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Woman, baby die after vessel overturns in New York Harbor

A vessel carrying 14 people overturned in New York Harbor near Liberty Island, resulting in the deaths of a woman and her 5-month-old baby. Authorities confirmed the boat's captain, Manuel Hernandez, was arrested for reckless endangerment. The New York Police Department responded to the incident around 10:25 p.m. to 10:55 p.m. on Saturday. Twelve people were rescued from the water before police arrived, with the woman and baby later found and taken to NYU Langone Hospital, where they were pronounced dead. Survivors were reported to have minor injuries and were taken to hospitals in stable condition. The Coast Guard is investigating whether the vessel operated illegally as a charter.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and UPI both identified the woman as Sara Sanchez and the baby as Antonella Garcia, while FOX News and The Daily Wire did not release their identities. UPI and the New York Post mentioned that the baby's father, who was Sanchez's boyfriend, was also on the boat, a detail not included in CBS News or FOX News. The New York Post and Straight Arrow News reported the boat was 21 feet or 22 feet long, while CBS News and UPI described it as a 2019 21-foot white Yamaha AR210 runabout. The New York Post and Straight Arrow News noted the boat was dangerously overloaded, a claim not made by CBS News or UPI. FOX News and The Daily Wire reported the boat was a 22-foot bowrider, while CBS News and UPI described it as a 21-foot runabout. The New York Post and Straight Arrow News stated the boat overturned around 10:30 p.m., while CBS News and UPI reported the time as 10:55 p.m. and 10:25 p.m., respectively.

Sources CBS News · FOX News · UPI · Straight Arrow News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump says Will Scharf will replace David Warrington as White House counsel in September

President Donald Trump announced that White House Staff Secretary Will Scharf will replace David Warrington as Assistant to the President and White House Counsel starting September 1. Trump praised Scharf for his legal background, including his work as a federal prosecutor and his representation of Trump in multiple cases, including at the Supreme Court. Scharf, who previously served as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, oversaw the approval of Trump’s $400 million White House ballroom project. The White House counsel’s role includes advising on legal and policy matters, coordinating with the Justice Department, and managing congressional investigations.

The White House counsel’s office is central to the administration’s legal strategy, handling presidential pardons, judicial appointments, and reviewing legislation. Scharf, who joined Trump’s legal team in October 2023, was involved in the presidential immunity case that led to the Supreme Court’s ruling in favor of Trump. The appointment comes amid preparations for the midterm elections, with Democrats vowing to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they gain control of Congress.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both mention that Scharf will replace Warrington effective September 1, while The Daily Wire and UPI state the effective date as September 1 as well. The Washington Examiner and ABC News note that Warrington is leaving for the private sector, though the Washington Examiner does not specify his new role, while ABC News and The Guardian describe him as returning to private practice. The Daily Wire and UPI mention that Scharf was part of the legal team that argued for Trump’s immunity in the Supreme Court case, while The Guardian and ABC News attribute this to Scharf’s involvement in the case. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both mention Scharf’s role in the National Capital Planning Commission, but The Washington Examiner adds that he led the commission, while The Guardian states he chaired it. The Daily Wire and UPI note that Scharf warned against suspending habeas corpus protections for illegal immigrants, a claim not made by The Guardian or ABC News.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · ABC News · UPI · The Guardian · Al Jazeera

Crews battle wildfires in western U.S. and Canada

Wildfires are spreading rapidly across the western U.S. and Canada, with evacuation orders in place for multiple regions. The National Interagency Fire Center reported 183 new fires, including eight large ones, across the U.S. since Saturday, with over 30,000 personnel and 640 crews assigned to the fires. In Utah, the Rocky Canyon Fire has grown to over 2,800 acres and is 0% contained, leading to evacuations in Morgan County. Two pilots died in a helicopter crash while battling the Widemouth 2 Fire in Fishlake National Forest, and the fire has scorched over 118,000 acres, becoming the largest in Utah this year. In Oregon, a bulldozer operator died while fighting the Wrights Spring Fire, which has spread over 33,000 acres. In Canada, British Columbia has seen over 100 wildfires, with the Bald Range wildfire prompting more than 20,000 people to evacuate. A state of emergency was declared in the province, and officials warned of "explosive" fire conditions due to prolonged drought and high temperatures.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and CBS News both report that the Widemouth 2 Fire has scorched over 118,000 acres and is the largest fire in Utah this year, surpassing the Babylon Fire. However, CBS News also mentions that the Bald Range wildfire has scorched more than 53 square miles, while BBC and UPI report it as 13,618 hectares (33,650 acres). The Guardian and CBS News state that an 80-year-old woman died while trying to escape the wildfire, while UPI and Washington Examiner confirm this death and attribute it to the Bald Range wildfire. The Guardian and CBS News also mention that the Bald Range fire was first detected late on Friday evening and grew to more than 40 sq miles within hours, while NPR and Washington Examiner report it as first reported Friday evening and growing to about 50 square kilometers within hours.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · CBS News · BBC · UPI · Washington Examiner

No source labeled right covered this story.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggs

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a 36-year-old New York congresswoman, announced she is freezing her eggs and will share the process online. She described the decision as a way to feel more in control of her life. Ocasio-Cortez shared the process through Instagram stories, showing the medication and tools used, including syringes and alcohol wipes. She injected herself in the dressing room before an ABC interview, stating that women can do anything and that it is “badass” to take such shots. She also mentioned the importance of normalizing conversations about women’s health, especially in a political environment where reproductive care is under threat.

Ocasio-Cortez emphasized the lack of information available to women about their bodies and reproductive health. She highlighted the challenges of balancing personal and political life, noting that being in the public eye at a young age means navigating major life decisions in the spotlight. She also mentioned the financial and technological advancements that have made egg freezing more accessible. Ocasio-Cortez hinted at the possibility of running for president in 2028, though she said the focus should remain on the midterm elections.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire both mention Ocasio-Cortez’s comments about the political “risk” of sharing her decision, while FOX News and The New York Post attribute similar statements to her. The Washington Examiner notes that Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a 2028 presidential run, a detail not included in The Guardian or BBC accounts. The Daily Wire and The New York Post describe Ocasio-Cortez as having been engaged to Riley Roberts since 2022, a detail absent from other accounts. The Guardian and The Daily Wire include quotes from Amanda Litman and Xochitl Hinojosa, which are not present in the Washington Examiner, BBC, or FOX News reports.

Sources The Guardian · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · BBC · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Shanghai cancels 1,300 flights as China prepares for Typhoon Dolphin

Typhoon Dolphin, which brought heavy rains to northern Taiwan, prompted authorities in China to cancel over 1,300 flights in Shanghai and relocate more than 300,000 people in surrounding regions. The storm’s outer bands hit northern Taiwan, including Taipei, on Saturday. Shanghai’s Hongqiao and Pudong airports canceled about 60% of Sunday’s expected flights. Authorities in Zhejiang province evacuated 390,000 people in Taizhou by Saturday evening and 900,000 in Wenzhou. In Fujian, 98,900 people were evacuated from high-risk areas. Forecasters warned of severe flooding and landslide risks, with some areas expected to receive 200-400 mm of rainfall over the next few days.

Authorities in Shanghai evacuated 30,000 people from riskier areas and suspended all water-based activities, including ferries and cruises. The storm’s maximum sustained winds were estimated at about 162 km/h (101 mph) as of Sunday morning. The National Meteorological Centre warned that the storm could slow over central and southwestern China, prolonging heavy rainfall and increasing flood and landslide risks.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Typhoon Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at 5:30pm on Sunday, with maximum sustained winds of 151 km/h (93 mph), equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane. This differs from the Associated Press, which states the storm’s maximum sustained winds were estimated at about 162 km/h (101 mph) as of Sunday morning. The Guardian also reports landfall at 5:30pm with 151 km/h winds, while UPI mentions landfall at Force 13 speeds of 85 mph. The Guardian also notes that Shanghai evacuated 215,600 people, substantially higher than the 30,300 figure cited by Al Jazeera and the BBC. The BBC mentions that Shanghai canceled nearly 1,000 flights, while the Associated Press and the Guardian report 1,300 and 1,500 flights canceled respectively.

Sources Associated Press · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian · UPI · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeños could hospitalize thousands, prompting recalls and economic losses for farmers.

Some meat products with jalapeños may be linked to salmonella outbreak, USDA says

Federal officials issued a public health alert for meat and poultry products containing jalapeños that may be contaminated with salmonella, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The alert applies to products regulated by the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) that may have been affected by a recalled ingredient. The USDA said it learned of the issue when it discovered that multiple FSIS-regulated establishments had received a recalled ingredient. The agency released a list of 18 recalled products, including brands like Taylor Farms, Ready Meals, Meal Simple, Higher Harvest, and Deli Kitchen. The USDA noted that additional downstream products may be identified as the ingredient recall progresses.

The salmonella outbreak was first reported in mid-June and is linked to jalapeño peppers grown in Sinaloa, Mexico, and distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors. As of Aug. 5, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that at least 345 people in 27 states had been sickened, with 36 hospitalized. Minnesota was particularly hard hit, with at least 110 cases confirmed. Of 191 patients interviewed, 93% reported eating at a Mexican-style restaurant before falling ill, including Chipotle and Qdoba. Both chains removed jalapeños from their menus. Albertsons voluntarily recalled four items containing jalapeños supplied by Taylor Farms.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News states that the USDA said there have been "no confirmed reports of illness" from FSIS-regulated products containing jalapeños sourced from Sinaloa. Straight Arrow News reports that FSIS said there have been "no confirmed illnesses tied specifically to the FSIS-regulated meat and poultry products containing the recalled jalapeños." CBS News also notes that the first illnesses were reported in mid-June and links them to jalapeños from Sinaloa, while Straight Arrow News attributes the outbreak to "fresh jalapeño peppers grown in Sinaloa, Mexico." CBS News mentions that Albertsons recalled four items, while Straight Arrow News states that the public health alert includes products sold under several brands and distributed through major retailers and convenience stores.

Sources CBS News · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Trump’s attorney general pick Todd Blanche appears to clear last hurdle for confirmation

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana announced on Friday that he will support Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, clearing the last major hurdle for the former Trump personal lawyer’s confirmation. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general, is expected to be confirmed by a narrow margin, likely along party lines, as the Senate prepares for its August recess. Cassidy, who lost his Louisiana primary in May, had faced pressure from the White House to back Blanche, citing concerns about “lawfare” at the Justice Department. With Cassidy’s support, Blanche’s confirmation now hinges on the votes of other Republicans, though Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska have already announced they will oppose the nomination.

Blanche’s confirmation has been complicated by concerns over his role in establishing the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund, which was part of a settlement with the IRS over Trump’s leaked tax returns. The fund was designed to compensate individuals who claimed they had been targeted by the federal government, including those convicted of assaulting law enforcement during the January 6 Capitol riot. Blanche issued a formal order on Sunday terminating the fund, following weeks of negotiations with Republican senators who had blocked his nomination. The Justice Department also agreed to grant Trump, his family, and affiliated entities immunity from tax audits and investigations as part of the same settlement.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that Cassidy’s support clears the last hurdle for Blanche’s confirmation, while NPR notes that the Senate vote was 50-49 in favor of Blanche. The Guardian and CBS News attribute Cassidy’s decision to concerns about “lawfare” at the Justice Department, while NPR and ABC News mention Cassidy’s concerns about Blanche’s judgment in exempting Trump from IRS audits and the DOJ’s prosecution of Trump’s political enemies. The Nation and Slate do not cover the confirmation process, focusing instead on Blanche’s potential policies on abortion and Hasan Piker’s political rise, respectively.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · NPR · ABC News · The Nation · Slate

Iran War Costs and Diplomatic Deadlock Amid Rising Tensions

The war between the United States and Iran has led to significant economic costs for American households and businesses, with fuel prices soaring and affecting everything from groceries to delivery services. According to Mother Jones, the U.S. has spent over $37.5 billion on the war, with additional costs expected to rise as the conflict continues. Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump have both expressed optimism about ongoing negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, though tensions remain high as Iran has issued new demands for a deal.

Iran has raised the stakes in peace talks by listing six conditions for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, including the lifting of sanctions and the withdrawal of U.S. military forces. These demands, reported by The Washington Examiner, Al Jazeera, and The New York Post, have complicated negotiations between Iran and Oman. Despite Trump’s public statements about progress, the situation remains unresolved, with the strait still closed and oil prices fluctuating.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that the U.S. has spent $37.5 billion on the war and that Americans have paid over $75 billion in additional fuel costs, while The Hill and The New York Post do not mention these figures. The Washington Examiner and Al Jazeera detail Iran’s six demands, including the lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen assets, which are not explicitly outlined in Mother Jones or The Hill. The Guardian provides a broader context of Trump’s inconsistent messaging and the political implications of the war, which are absent in the other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · The Washington Examiner · The New York Post · Al Jazeera · The Guardian

U.S. pledges $1B to Colombia's new right-wing president

The U.S. Department of State announced plans to provide $1 billion in security assistance to Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, following his inauguration. De la Espriella, a right-wing lawyer and businessman, won the June 21 runoff election against leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda by 250,000 votes out of over 26 million cast. His campaign promised an "all-out war" on drug cartels, a 40% reduction in government size, and revitalization of the oil and gas sector. In his inaugural speech, he vowed to "relentlessly defeat narco-terrorism" and ensure "there will not be a single place in our territory where criminals can feel safe." The U.S. delegation, led by acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, attended the inauguration in Cali, Colombia, where de la Espriella also pledged to join the Shield of the Americas, a U.S.-backed regional security initiative.

Where the accounts differ

UPI and The Guardian both report that the U.S. pledged $1 billion in security assistance to de la Espriella's administration. However, CBS News and BBC mention the pledge was made on the first day of his presidency, while UPI and The Guardian specify it was announced after his inauguration. Al Jazeera and FOX News do not mention the exact timing of the $1 billion pledge. Additionally, The Guardian and BBC note that de la Espriella's election is part of a broader rightward shift in Latin America, a detail not included in UPI or CBS News. FOX News and CBS News both mention that de la Espriella received Trump's endorsement, while UPI and The Guardian attribute this to Trump's support for his campaign. Al Jazeera and BBC do not mention Trump's endorsement explicitly.

Sources UPI · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · FOX News · CBS News · BBC

Russian strikes near Ukrainian capital kill three, including child

Russian strikes have killed three people, including a child, in the region surrounding Kyiv, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. A grandfather, grandmother and their 3-year-old grandson were killed by a double-tap drone strike in Pukhivka, in the Brovary District. The child’s parents, his 15-year-old brother and a neighbor who came to the family’s aid were wounded. Zelenskyy also reported one additional death in Kyiv from a strike involving six ballistic missiles. Ukraine’s air force said it had downed or intercepted 135 of 151 drones launched by Russia overnight. The attack also involved six ballistic missiles and other guided missiles. Russian attacks have intensified, with Ukraine’s air defenses struggling to keep up. Zelenskyy has called for more Patriot interceptors and sanctions against Russia. Ukraine has also targeted Russian oil refineries and logistics sites.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and UPI both report that a 3-year-old child was killed, while Associated Press and CBS News refer to a child without specifying age. Associated Press and CBS News mention that four people were killed, including the child, while Al Jazeera and UPI report three people killed, including the child. Associated Press and CBS News state that one additional person died in Kyiv from a strike involving six ballistic missiles, while Al Jazeera and UPI do not mention this. UPI and CBS News attribute the statement about the strike involving six ballistic missiles to Zelenskyy, while Al Jazeera and Associated Press do not attribute the statement. ABC News and BBC do not mention the specific number of casualties in the Kyiv area beyond the family in Brovary District.

Sources Al Jazeera · Associated Press · BBC · ABC News · UPI · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Idaho police release video of In-N-Out Burger mass shooting that killed three

Police released video on Friday of a mass shooting that killed three people at an Idaho In-N-Out Burger restaurant last weekend. The video, edited to blur faces and omit graphic images, showed the gunman, identified as Chad Williams, 24, walking up to the drive-thru window four times and opening fire, killing an In-N-Out employee. Ten people were shot during the incident, with three people killed. Williams, who had previously lived in Arizona and briefly attended the College of Southern Idaho, killed himself when police officers caught up to him on a nearby walking trail. Authorities praised an unarmed employee from a nearby store who engaged the gunman outdoors, slowing him down and possibly preventing more deaths, as well as an off-duty state trooper and a former police officer, AJ James, who were wounded while confronting him.

The video also showed that at least three people confronted the gunman with their own weapons during the incident. One of those individuals, Braxton Steube, who was working at a Dick’s Sporting Goods store near the scene, told KMVT-TV that he encountered Williams on the trail after fleeing the store. Steube said he tried to talk to the gunman, who eventually shot at him and missed. The video also showed that an armed civilian, identified by some outlets as Jordan Salinas, confronted the gunman at a Tesla charging station, and that the gunman shot Dale Schultz, 66, of Salt Lake City, and wounded his wife.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that the gunman shot Ashley Garibay, 23, of Stockton, California, at the drive-thru window, and that he later shot Christopher Claunch, 59, of Hagerman, Idaho, in his vehicle. The Guardian and The Daily Wire both mention that Williams killed himself when police caught up to him on a nearby walking trail, while FOX News and CBS News state that he died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that Williams had briefly attended the College of Southern Idaho and previously lived in Arizona, while FOX News and CBS News do not mention this. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also report that an unnamed individual found Williams’ discarded handgun at a Tesla charging station, while FOX News and CBS News do not mention this. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that Williams shot Terry Dudley twice in the back while charging his vehicle, while FOX News and CBS News do not mention this.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

The US lost 23,000 jobs in July. Here’s why unemployment didn’t rise.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm employers cut 23,000 jobs in July, below the 80,000 jobs economists had anticipated. At the same time, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, but this was attributed to a shrinking labor force rather than increased employment. The labor force declined by 264,000 people, with job losses concentrated in local government education and retail sectors. Healthcare added 22,000 jobs, while the private sector gained 30,000 jobs overall. Analysts note that the labor force has remained at 158 million for 21 months, the longest streak at a single number in BLS records. The drop in job creation has raised concerns about slowing economic growth, with some economists suggesting that the labor market may be near zero growth.

Where the accounts differ

The Christian Science Monitor and the Guardian both mention that the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% due to a shrinking labor force, but the Guardian adds that the private sector gained 30,000 jobs, while the Christian Science Monitor attributes the drop in unemployment to a decline in the labor force of 264,000. The Mother Jones article attributes the job losses to employers’ wariness amid tariffs and the war in Iran, while the BBC and CBS News cite the summer slump and seasonal factors. The Guardian and CBS News both mention that the labor force participation rate fell to 61.4%, the lowest since February 2021, while the Christian Science Monitor does not mention this decline. The BBC and CBS News also note that the May and June job figures were revised down by 103,000, a detail not included in the Christian Science Monitor or the Guardian.

Sources Christian Science Monitor · Mother Jones · BBC · The Guardian · NPR · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Helicopter fighting Utah wildfire crashes with two people onboard, officials say

A firefighting Sikorsky S64 helicopter with two individuals onboard crashed on Friday morning in a remote area of central Utah, according to federal aviation authorities. Emergency personnel are responding near Richfield, about 160 miles south of Salt Lake City. The exact circumstances surrounding the crash are unknown. The aircraft was in the vicinity of the Widemouth 2 fire, a blaze sparked by lightning that has raced through 105,000 acres since it began on 27 July. As of Friday morning, the fire was 19% contained with 632 personnel assigned to suppressing it, and seven helicopters were dropping retardant and water on the flames.

The crash comes amid a deadly wildfire season for the western US. Three firefighters were killed in June as they battled a blaze along the Colorado-Utah border. In late June, Jamie Barnes, the director of Utah’s division of forestry, described the fires as unlike anything in recent memory. “We’re seeing fires spread farther and faster under conditions that defy historical expectations,” Barnes said. “Our firefighters have been working around the clock, our resources are stretched, and we cannot afford preventable ignitions during the days ahead.”

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News report that no word was given on the condition of the two people onboard at the time of the crash, while The New York Post and Al Jazeera state that the two individuals were confirmed dead. The New York Post and Al Jazeera attribute the confirmation of deaths to the Sevier County Sheriff, while The Guardian and CBS News do not specify who confirmed the deaths. The New York Post and Al Jazeera mention the crash ignited a new fire that connected with the existing blaze, while The Guardian and CBS News do not include this detail. The Guardian and CBS News report the fire was 19% contained, while Al Jazeera reports containment at 24% and The New York Post reports the fire had scorched nearly 174 square miles.

Sources The Guardian · UPI · New York Post · Al Jazeera · CBS News · The Guardian

Todd Blanche narrowly confirmed as Trump’s attorney general in overnight vote

The Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general in a vote early Saturday morning, cementing President Donald Trump’s former personal attorney’s command of a Justice Department the Republican president has sought to bend to his will. The Republican-led Senate voted 50-49 to make Blanche the second confirmed attorney general since Trump returned to the White House last year with a stated desire to use the law enforcement agency to investigate his political enemies. While Blanche has already been leading the department in an acting capacity, his confirmation could free him to pursue the Trump administration’s agenda even more aggressively. The vote followed a tumultuous confirmation fight that exposed deep concerns — from some Republicans as well as Democrats — about installing Trump’s close ally atop a Justice Department that historically prided itself on its independence from the White House.

Blanche’s confirmation hinged on the support of Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who announced his decision to vote for Blanche on Friday morning. Cassidy said the decision was not a referendum on Trump but rather a judgment about whether Blanche would be able to effectively lead the agency and provide legal counsel to the president. He acknowledged concerns about Blanche’s role in a controversial settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS, which included a proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund for Trump’s allies and an exemption from federal tax audits. Blanche publicly promised to abandon the fund and rein in the settlement’s other provisions.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and The Hill both report that Blanche’s confirmation was 50-49, while The Daily Wire and The Hill mention that Blanche’s confirmation was narrowly secured with Cassidy’s support. The BBC and The Hill note that Senator Lisa Murkowski opposed Blanche’s confirmation, citing concerns over the “politicisation” of the justice department. The Daily Wire and The Hill also mention that Senator Susan Collins opposed Blanche’s confirmation, citing concerns over the independence of the Justice Department. The Associated Press and The Hill report that Blanche publicly promised to abandon the $1.8 billion fund and rein in the settlement’s other provisions, while the BBC and The Daily Wire attribute these promises to Blanche.

Sources Associated Press · BBC · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Axios · The Hill

Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police say

A 14-year-old student opened fire at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Nonthaburi province, killing at least five people and taking his own life, according to Thai police. The suspected attacker also killed his grandparents before the shooting, authorities said. The incident left more than 30 people injured, with nine in critical condition. The school was locked down for about half an hour before police arrived. Teachers and students were evacuated, with some leaving their shoes behind in the rush. The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, vowed to implement new gun laws, though details were not provided. Thailand has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in Southeast Asia, and past efforts to tighten gun laws have not prevented repeated shootings.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and UPI both report that the suspected attacker killed his grandparents before the school shooting, while Newsweek and CBS News do not specify the grandparents were killed. The Guardian and UPI state the attacker killed himself, while ABC News and CBS News also mention the suspect died by suicide. The Guardian and UPI report that the attacker used a 9mm handgun, while the Guardian and CBS News mention the attacker had 26 bullets fired and 34 rounds recovered. The Guardian and UPI report that the prime minister did not provide specifics on the new gun law, while ABC News and CBS News mention the prime minister said the law would restrict gun ownership to government officials on duty. The Guardian and UPI report that the shooter had 34 additional ammunition rounds, while CBS News and UPI mention the shooter had 34 rounds recovered. The Guardian and UPI report that the shooter had 26 bullets fired, while CBS News and UPI mention the shooter had 26 bullets fired. The Guardian and UPI report that the shooter had 34 rounds recovered, while CBS News and UPI mention the shooter had 34 rounds recovered. The Guardian and UPI report that the shooter had 26 bullets fired, while CBS News and UPI mention the shooter had 26 bullets fired. The Guardian and UPI report that the shooter had 34 rounds recovered, while CBS News and UPI mention the shooter had 34 rounds recovered.

Sources The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · Newsweek · UPI · Associated Press

Abdul El-Sayed narrowly wins Michigan Democratic Senate primary

Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive physician and former public health official, won the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan by less than 16,000 votes, overcoming a massive outside spending effort. His campaign rejected corporate PAC money, while his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, received over $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s United Democracy Project super PAC. El-Sayed’s victory has sparked internal debate within the Democratic Party over the viability of progressive candidates in statewide races. Political strategist David Axelrod, a former Obama adviser, acknowledged the win as impressive given the financial disadvantage but noted El-Sayed’s need to focus on issues like economic security rather than more radical positions. Meanwhile, Republican nominee Mike Rogers, who previously criticized Donald Trump, has launched a campaign targeting moderate Democrats, framing El-Sayed’s victory as a sign of a “divisive” movement.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Nation differ on the nature of El-Sayed’s platform and its implications. The Daily Wire claims El-Sayed is not a democratic socialist but holds many of the radical party’s viewpoints, including calls to abolish ICE and defund the police, and notes he has campaigned with communist influencer Hasan Piker. The Nation, however, portrays El-Sayed as a pro-Palestine candidate who ran on a platform centering Palestinian humanity and opposing U.S. military funding to Israel, and highlights his victory as a landmark moment for the Palestine movement. The Daily Wire also states El-Sayed wiped social media posts advocating for defunding the police, while The Nation does not mention this. The New York Post and The Nation both note El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel, but only The Nation frames it as part of a broader pro-Palestine movement.

Sources NPR · The Daily Wire · Slate · New York Post · FOX News · The Nation

No source labeled center covered this story.

US Senate passes sweeping Russian energy sanctions bill amid Ukraine war

The US Senate passed a sanctions bill targeting Russia’s energy revenues amid its invasion of Ukraine. The legislation, named the “Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” includes tariffs on Russian oil and gas imports. The bill passed with a vote of 86–11, sending it to the House of Representatives. The measure aims to cut off financial support for Russia’s war efforts by imposing tariffs on major importers, including China and India. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the move, calling it a significant step toward ending the war. The bill also extends sanctions against Iran, targeting its energy and weapons sectors. The Russian Embassy in Washington condemned the legislation, citing potential energy constraints and rising gas prices in the US.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both report the bill includes tariffs of up to 100% on major importers, but The Guardian adds that the bill allows Donald Trump to impose levies of up to 500% on Russian exports. The Hill and UPI mention the bill includes an exception for countries importing less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia, which is not stated in Al Jazeera or The Guardian. FOX News reports the bill includes tariffs of up to 500% on Russian imports, a detail not included in other accounts. The Guardian and The Hill note that the bill was named in honor of Lindsey Graham, while Al Jazeera and UPI also mention the naming but do not specify the reason. The Hill and FOX News mention the inclusion of Iran sanctions at the request of Trump, which is not explicitly stated in Al Jazeera or The Guardian.

Sources Al Jazeera · The Guardian · The Hill · UPI · NPR · FOX News

Pentagon revokes ex-Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall’s security clearance over Air Force One comments

The Pentagon revoked former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall’s access to classified information, citing unauthorized disclosure of information about Air Force One’s capabilities to a media outlet. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell announced the revocation on X, stating that safeguarding classified information is a non-negotiable duty. Kendall served under President Joe Biden and retained his security clearance after leaving office. The statement did not specify which comments prompted the revocation, though Kendall had previously questioned the security capabilities of the new Qatari-gifted jet. The White House has defended the new Air Force One, calling it secure and equipped with high-level security protocols.

Kendall made public comments in July about the new jet, suggesting that significant modifications would take three to four years to complete and that a one-month refit period was insufficient for major hardware changes. He also expressed doubts about whether the plane had been adequately modified. The White House has pushed back against these comments, with communications director Steven Cheung asserting that the new Air Force One is secure. The Pentagon has also cited concerns raised by the New York Times about the plane’s lack of advanced security features, including antimissile capabilities.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and CBS News both mention that the Pentagon did not specify which media outlet Kendall was accused of sharing classified information with. The UPI and FOX News state that the Pentagon did not identify the media outlet. The New York Post and CBS News note that the Trump administration subpoenaed New York Times journalists after the outlet reported on security concerns with the Qatari-gifted jet. The Washington Examiner and CBS News also mention that the White House has pushed back against Kendall’s comments, while the New York Post and UPI include details about the Trump administration’s legal actions against the Times. The Just The News and FOX News do not mention the subpoenas or the White House’s response to Kendall’s comments.

Sources Washington Examiner · New York Post · CBS News · UPI · Just The News · FOX News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Trump revives effort to fire Governor Lisa Cook from the Fed

President Donald Trump is once again attempting to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, citing mortgage fraud allegations. The White House has sent a letter to Cook demanding a written response within 21 days, following a Supreme Court ruling that required notice and an opportunity to respond before removal. The letter, obtained by multiple outlets, claims there is "sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements." The Supreme Court previously blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook in June, ruling that the president could not remove a Fed member without proper justification.

Cook's legal team, including Abbe Lowell, has called the allegations "as baseless now as they were a year ago," arguing that the claims are part of a "manufactured pretext" to interfere with the Fed's independence. The White House has not provided specific details about the nature of the mortgage fraud allegations, though they were initially raised by Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, who submitted a criminal referral to the Justice Department.

Where the accounts differ

UPI and Fox Business both report that the White House letter was obtained by Politico and ABC News, respectively. UPI states that the letter was obtained by Politico, while Fox Business says it was first reported by ABC News. The Guardian and NPR both mention that the letter was first reported by ABC News, but the Guardian adds that the letter was "first reported by ABC News" and that the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Guardian also notes that Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022, a detail not included in the other accounts. UPI and Fox Business both mention that the Supreme Court ruled in June that the president could not remove a Fed member without proper justification, but Fox Business adds that the court's opinion emphasized that the president could not remove a Fed member "at any time, for any reason, without any notice before, and without any judicial check after."

Sources UPI · Fox Business · Axios · ABC News · The Guardian · NPR

No source labeled right covered this story.

US appeals court halts Trump ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown

A federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration cannot proceed with above-ground construction of a planned White House ballroom without congressional approval. The three-judge panel, in a 2-1 decision, stated that the White House is not the property of any single president but belongs to the American people. The ruling upheld a lower court order blocking above-ground work, while allowing underground construction to continue. The administration has appealed the decision to the Supreme Court, which has stayed the ruling for 14 days. President Trump criticized the decision as "horrendous" and "politically motivated," vowing to have it overturned. The project, which includes a 90,000-square-foot ballroom and security infrastructure, has faced legal challenges since October when the East Wing was demolished to make way for the new structure. The National Trust for Historic Preservation supported the ruling, arguing that the White House should not be altered without congressional approval.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the administration appealed to the court after a federal judge twice blocked above-ground construction, while still allowing underground work to proceed. The Daily Wire states that the court allowed below-ground construction to continue, including work related to security infrastructure. ABC News mentions that the ruling does not take effect for two weeks, allowing time for the Trump administration to appeal. CBS News notes that the court stayed its decision for 14 days. FOX News highlights that Trump accused the court of refusing to acknowledge that the ballroom is being built ahead of schedule and under budget. The Daily Caller states that the court paused its order for two weeks to allow for the administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · ABC News · CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Caller

US intel warns Russia could launch limited attack on NATO ally in effort to fragment organization: report

U.S. intelligence has warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin may attempt to test NATO's unity by launching a limited attack or hybrid operation against a NATO member state in the coming years. The assessment, reported by The Wall Street Journal, suggests such an attack could range from a cyberattack to a small-scale land incursion, with a focus on the Baltics or Poland. The U.S. and European allies have noted increased signs that Russia is probing NATO's response capabilities. A drone attack on a Romanian apartment building in May and cruise missiles landing in Poland last month are cited as recent examples of Russia's probing tactics.

The discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig, Germany’s airport has also raised concerns. German officials say the drone was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane carrying military ammunition, and the incident is being treated as part of a "professional hybrid threat scenario" involving foreign powers. The drone, which had a non-functional detonator, was discovered before it could detonate, potentially averting a catastrophe. The incident has led to the suspension of air traffic at the airport and is being investigated for possible links to Russian intelligence.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the U.S. intelligence assessment suggests Russia may test NATO by launching a limited attack, while The Guardian and Washington Examiner connect the Leipzig drone incident to potential Russian involvement. The Guardian and Washington Examiner attribute the drone discovery to a possible Russian plot, whereas CBS News and Straight Arrow News link the incident to broader Russian hybrid operations. The Guardian and Washington Examiner also note the drone had a non-functional detonator, a detail not mentioned in FOX News or CBS News. Straight Arrow News adds that the drone was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane carrying military ammunition, a detail not included in other accounts.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · BBC · Washington Examiner · CBS News · Straight Arrow News

Court orders Instagram and Facebook's Meta to pay $567M to address kids' mental health online

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, to pay $567 million to address harms to young people from its platforms. The ruling comes in the second phase of a landmark trial, following a March jury decision that found Meta knowingly harmed children's mental health and concealed knowledge about child sexual exploitation. The total amount Meta is responsible for — $942 million — includes the $375 million in civil penalties from the first phase. The court ordered the bulk of the money, $420 million, to be used for treatment services for young people, with the remainder allocated for awareness, prevention, and screening services over the next five years. The ruling also mandates changes to Meta's platforms, including the implementation of informational screens, improved age assurance tools, and restrictions on adult contact with minors.

The court found that federal children's privacy laws prevent Meta from applying age-verification tools to children under 13. Instead, Meta must continue to improve its age-assurance tools, using artificial intelligence to estimate age based on user data. The company is also required to request proof of age for users in New Mexico it estimates to be under 13 and delete personal information collected on users under 13. Meta must partner with schools or child safety organizations to create a reporting portal for flagging underage users and report on its progress twice a year.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both report that the court ordered Meta to pay $567 million and that the total liability is $942 million, including the $375 million from the first phase. Al Jazeera and CBS News also mention the $567 million and $942 million total, but Al Jazeera notes that the ruling comes in the second phase of a landmark trial, while CBS News refers to it as the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March. UPI adds that the court found Meta created a public nuisance and that the case was bifurcated into two phases, with Phase 1 being a jury trial and Phase 2 a bench trial. Fox Business states that the $567 million is on top of the $375 million in civil penalties and that the court found Meta created a public nuisance, with specific details about the youth-safety measures ordered.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · CBS News · UPI · Fox Business

Chuck Edwards' abrupt exit leaves Republicans scrambling

Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) abruptly withdrew from his re-election campaign after the House Ethics Committee recommended his censure for violating House rules over sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment. Edwards' decision came after the committee's findings, which included incidents of harassment and inappropriate conduct toward female staffers, were made public. His exit has complicated the Republican strategy for the 11th District, which was already a toss-up race. Democratic opponent Jamie Ager significantly out-raised Edwards in the second quarter, shifting the race from "lean Republican" to "toss-up" according to Sabato's Crystal Ball. Edwards' withdrawal has weakened the GOP position, with some Republicans acknowledging the seat is now in trouble. The replacement nominee will have to start from scratch three months before Election Day, requiring significant fundraising efforts from the GOP.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Edwards' decision to drop out was made via social media, while The Hill notes that the House Ethics Committee's findings were corroborated by Axios and included handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, and other incidents. The Daily Wire and Mother Jones focus on different representatives, Max Miller, and his allegations of abuse, which are not mentioned in Axios or The Hill. The Daily Caller and New York Post discuss Cory Mills' political troubles and primary challenges, which are not covered in the other accounts. The Hill and Axios both mention the House Democratic Women’s Caucus calling for Edwards' resignation, but The Hill adds that the Democratic Women’s Caucus is working on a bipartisan measure to prohibit romantic relationships between members of Congress and all staffers.

Sources Axios · The Hill · The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · New York Post · The Daily Caller

Senate panel votes to hold Dr. Fauci in contempt over refusal to answer questions

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted Thursday to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress for repeatedly invoking the Fifth Amendment during a hearing last week. The vote, which was 8-5, followed Fauci’s refusal to answer questions about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic and his role in the federal response. Rand Paul, the committee’s chairman, said he would immediately refer the contempt resolution to the Department of Justice for possible prosecution. Fauci, who was pardoned by President Joe Biden before leaving office, argued that the Fifth Amendment still protected him from self-incrimination. Democrats criticized the vote as a political stunt that could harm future oversight efforts.

Paul claimed that Fauci had no legal basis to invoke the Fifth Amendment because of the pardon, which he said covers any crimes committed from 2014 to 2025. Fauci’s attorneys argued that the pardon only protects against federal crimes and does not negate his Fifth Amendment rights. The Department of Justice has not yet commented on whether it will investigate the referral.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and ABC News both state that Paul plans to send the contempt resolution directly to the Department of Justice, while The Hill and Axios note that the resolution could also be sent to the full Senate for a vote. The Daily Wire mentions that Paul’s office sent two criminal referrals to the Biden Justice Department and two more under Trump, while The Hill and Axios do not specify the number of referrals. The Daily Wire also includes details about the potential prison sentences for Bannon and Navarro, which are not mentioned in the other accounts. The Hill and Axios describe the legal argument around the pardon and the Fifth Amendment, while The Daily Wire attributes the characterization of the pardon as a "sweeping" one to Paul.

Sources The Daily Wire · Axios · Just The News · The Hill · NPR · ABC News

Sen. Mitch McConnell Gives Major Update After Months In Hospital

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) announced Thursday that he has been released from a rehabilitation facility and will continue his recovery at his Kentucky home, ending a months-long hospitalization. The 84-year-old senator, who is not running for reelection, provided no timeline on a possible return to Washington, D.C. His absence has complicated efforts to confirm Todd Blanche’s nomination to be the U.S. Attorney General, as the acting Attorney General is struggling to earn 50 votes for confirmation. McConnell stated he will maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period and continue to engage with his staff and colleagues on important Senate business.

McConnell’s extended hospitalization has fueled questions about his health and what would happen if he were unable to complete his final term. He has remained hospitalized since June 14, when emergency responders were dispatched to his Washington residence following what was widely reported as an emergency radio traffic describing a cardiac arrest requiring CPR. The lack of information sparked widespread speculation online. The Kentucky Republican’s absence has also drawn scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties, with Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, publicly urging McConnell to release more information about his health.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Guardian both state that McConnell was hospitalized following a fall at home in June and that he was briefly unconscious. The New York Post and The Daily Caller mention that McConnell was found “unconscious” and taken to the hospital in an ambulance, while The Daily Wire and The Guardian do not specify the exact nature of the emergency. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note that McConnell’s office initially provided few details, while The New York Post and The Daily Caller include quotes from McConnell’s July 12 statement, which he said he had been hospitalized due to a fall and a “mild case of pneumonia.” The Daily Wire and The Guardian also mention that McConnell’s doctors have stated he is not yet medically cleared to return to the office, while The New York Post and The Daily Caller do not include this detail. The Daily Wire and The Guardian report that McConnell’s absence has complicated the confirmation of Todd Blanche, while The New York Post and The Daily Caller do not mention this explicitly.

Sources The Daily Wire · Axios · The Guardian · New York Post · The Daily Caller · ABC News

Trump says he hasn't made a determination on Pirro's future

President Trump stated Tuesday he has not decided whether to retain Jeanine Pirro as U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia after she dropped charges against Olympian David Hearn for allegedly damaging the Reflecting Pool. Pirro cited contractor issues as the cause of the damage, not Hearn. The case was dismissed by a D.C. judge, with Pirro’s office citing insufficient information from the Department of Interior. Trump criticized Pirro publicly, calling her performance in court “vicious” and accusing her of “choking.” Meanwhile, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed a lawsuit against the Department of Justice, alleging the agency is withholding Epstein-related records needed for a state investigation into Zorro Ranch.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche faced scrutiny over his handling of the Epstein files, with Torrez accusing the DOJ of “stonewalling” the state’s investigation. The lawsuit claims the DOJ provided only 31 pages of materials, far less than the 13,000 mentions of Zorro Ranch in the files. Blanche’s comments on abortion rights, including plans to restrict access even in states where it is legal, were also reported, though the Justice Department said his remarks were mischaracterized.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and UPI both report that Pirro dropped charges against Hearn, citing contractor issues, while The Guardian and Christian Science Monitor note that the case was dismissed by a judge. The Hill and UPI describe Trump’s public criticism of Pirro, while The Guardian and Christian Science Monitor attribute the dismissal of the case to the judge’s decision. The Guardian and Christian Science Monitor report that the DOJ provided only 31 pages of materials, while ABC News and The Guardian mention that the DOJ provided some documents but not the full set. The Hill and UPI report that Trump called Pirro “vicious” and accused her of “choking,” while The Guardian and Christian Science Monitor do not include this specific language.

Sources The Hill · ABC News · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · UPI · Christian Science Monitor
