Rep. Max Miller denies abuse allegations, ex-father-in-law Sen. Bernie Moreno calls for resignation

Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) denied allegations of domestic abuse against his ex-wife and daughter in a livestream on X, stating no court or agency has substantiated the claims. Miller claimed child-welfare agencies found reports of abuse against his daughter unsubstantiated. He also denied assaulting his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who had previously accused him of throwing hot water at her during a 2024 argument. Miller acknowledged spraying her with water but denied it was scalding. He said he did not intend to hurt her and called the incident "horseplay."

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), Miller's ex-father-in-law, publicly denounced Miller as a "danger" to his daughter and unfit for office. Moreno described the situation as "pure hell" for his family and said Miller's behavior had forced him to speak out. He called for Miller to seek professional help and argued that the congressman should not be free to continue endangering others until he does. Moreno also mentioned that prosecutors did not file charges after concluding there was "insufficient admissible evidence" to present to a grand jury.

Miller faces Democrat Brian Poindexter in Ohio's 7th congressional district. The race is significant for Democrats, who view the seat as a potential pickup. Miller's campaign has been scrutinized for its handling of the allegations, with some Republicans expressing concern about the political fallout.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Miller acknowledged spraying his ex-wife with water but denied it was scalding, while The Daily Caller and The Guardian describe the incident as Miller throwing "scalding water" on Emily Moreno. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that Emily Moreno testified that Miller held a gun to her head, a detail not included in Axios or Mother Jones. The Guardian and The Daily Wire note that Emily Moreno alleges Miller broke their daughter’s collarbone, while Axios and Mother Jones describe the injury as resulting from a custody exchange and mention that police concluded there was "insufficient admissible evidence" to present to a grand jury. Mother Jones and The Guardian report that Miller has been accused of throwing a woman down the stairs in 2021, a claim not mentioned in Axios or The Daily Caller.

Sources Axios · The Daily Caller · Mother Jones · The Guardian · The Daily Wire · ABC News

Eastern Washington fires destroy 600 structures and force 60,000 to evacuate

Wildfires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area while destroying at least 600 homes, businesses and other structures, authorities said. The fires in and around Spokane burned about 8.2 sq miles, but they were among dozens across the western US that stretched the ability of federal, state and local agencies to fight them. Officials said the evacuees in Spokane included patients at its US Veterans Affairs hospital. The National Weather Service issued warnings about the air quality in eastern Washington, eastern Oregon, western and central Idaho and western Montana. It issued red flag fire warnings for parts of Utah and Montana and western Nebraska, and extreme heat warnings for the southern parts of Arizona, California and Nevada and northern Montana.

The fires in Spokane were part of a larger pattern of wildfires across the Pacific Northwest, with 99 large fires burning in the U.S. as of Sunday. Washington had 17 active large fires, including three major blazes in the Spokane area that forced evacuations and knocked out power to thousands. Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency, citing drought conditions, high temperatures and high winds. The Old Trails Fire, one of the three in Spokane, started around noon on Saturday and burned over 3,500 acres by early Sunday morning, according to the Washington State Department of Natural Resources.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Associated Press both report that the Old Trails Fire started around noon on Saturday and burned over 3,500 acres by early Sunday morning. The Guardian states that the fires in Spokane burned about 8.2 sq miles, while the Associated Press says the Old Trails Fire had burned over 3,500 acres by early Sunday morning. The Washington Examiner claims that more than 200,000 acres are burning in 12 large fires across eastern Washington, a figure not mentioned by other outlets. The Associated Press and NPR both mention that the Old Trails Fire burned at Riverside State Park, to the northwest of Spokane, while the Guardian does not specify the location of the Old Trails Fire. The Guardian and NPR both report that the fires in Spokane burned about 8.2 sq miles, while the Associated Press says the Old Trails Fire had burned over 3,500 acres by early Sunday morning.

Sources The Guardian · Associated Press · Washington Examiner · NPR · Axios · UPI

Top mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in Pakistan

Nirmal Purja, a British-Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member, died after being among 11 climbers caught in an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. The incident occurred on Thursday, with rescuers confirming the deaths of multiple climbers. Elite Exped, the company Purja co-founded, stated that Purja and other members of the expedition did not survive. The expedition included climbers from Nepal, the US, Oman, Pakistan, China, and another foreign national. The avalanche struck near camps two and three on the west ridge of the 8,047-metre mountain, according to GPS data. Rescue efforts faced challenges due to harsh weather conditions, with some bodies recovered but others still missing.

Purja, known as Nimsdai, was celebrated for climbing all 14 of the world’s peaks over 8,000 metres in 189 days in 2019. He also led the first team to summit K2 in winter. The expedition included notable climbers such as Nadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, and Mallory Geis, an American climber. Purja’s company confirmed the deaths of other climbers, including his climbing partners and guides, such as Pur Bahadur Gurung and Nima Sherpa. The British adventurer Bear Grylls expressed grief over Purja’s death, highlighting his impact on the climbing community.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both mention that the avalanche struck at around noon on Thursday, while the UPI account states the avalanche occurred on Thursday but does not specify the time. The Guardian and NPR report that four bodies were found by Friday, while CBS News and FOX News mention three bodies found by Friday. The Guardian and CBS News list Mallory Geis as the American climber, while FOX News refers to her as Sarah Mallory Geis. The Guardian and NPR identify Nadhira Alharthy as the first Omani to climb Everest, while the UPI and CBS News refer to her as Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy. The Guardian and CBS News mention that Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta) and Nima Sherpa died, while the UPI and FOX News list Pur Bahadur Gurung as Yukta and Nima Sherpa as one of the deceased.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · CBS News · BBC · UPI · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Water-dropping aircraft take off to tackle major Greek wildfire, after 2 killed in crash

Five water-dropping planes and five helicopters took off at first light Monday to assist hundreds of firefighters battling a major wildfire west of Athens, Greece, a day after a midair collision between two firefighting helicopters killed two crew members. The collision highlighted the dangers of fighting wildfires in volatile conditions. Flames advanced deeper into the region of the Greek capital, prompting fresh evacuations. In France, firefighters guarded a still-burning scar four times the size of Paris. The two crew members — one Greek and one Danish national — died when their helicopter collided with another near the seaside area of Psatha while tackling the fire that started Friday morning. The blaze raged through pine forests and scrubland through the weekend, whipped by gale force winds that often prevented water-dropping planes from operating. The crew of the second helicopter – a Greek and a British national – were taken to a hospital, where their injuries were reported to be light.

Greece’s firefighting department said the fire apparently began from sparks emitted by a faulty power line transporting electricity from a private wind generator facility to the main electricity network. Two people were arrested — an electrical engineer responsible for designing and overseeing the power project, and a contractor involved in constructing the electricity transmission network. Both face felony arson charges, while authorities had also issued an arrest warrant for the owner of the wind generator company.

Where the accounts differ

AP and UPI both state that two crew members died in the collision, with one being a Greek national and the other a Danish national. BBC and Straight Arrow News add that the second helicopter had a British pilot and a Greek co-ordinator who survived. CBS News and The Guardian do not mention the British survivor. The Guardian and BBC attribute the collision to two Bell helicopters leased from Australian company McDermott Aviation, while AP and UPI do not specify the helicopter model. Straight Arrow News and The Guardian mention that the collision occurred in the Psatha area of western Attica, while CBS News and AP refer to the area as near Porto Germeno. UPI and Straight Arrow News report that more than 16,000 acres have been burned by multiple fires on the Gulf of Corinth, while AP and CBS News do not provide this figure.

Sources Associated Press · CBS News · The Guardian · UPI · Straight Arrow News · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Sopranos actor Vincent Pastore, known for playing mobsters and tough guys, dies aged 80

Vincent Pastore, a veteran actor known for his roles as mobsters and tough guys, has died at the age of 80. He was best known for playing Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero on the TV series *The Sopranos*. His manager, Bob McGowan, confirmed his death, stating that Pastore was found in his home on New York’s City Island after not being heard from for several days. Pastore had a long acting career, appearing in films such as *Goodfellas* and *Awakenings*, and had a role in the 1990s TV series *The Sopranos*. He was born in the Bronx and grew up in suburban New Rochelle, New York. He enlisted in the Navy during the Vietnam War and later attended Pace University. He is survived by his daughter, Renee Pastore.

Pastore’s career spanned several decades, with roles in television series such as *Law & Order*, *Blue Bloods*, and *General Hospital*. He also appeared in films like *Carlito's Way* and *Men of Respect*. His role as “Big Pussy” on *The Sopranos* brought him widespread recognition, though his character was killed off in the second season. Pastore returned for several guest appearances in later seasons. His manager, Robert Attermann, described him as a kind and generous person who supported young actors and was passionate about his craft. Friends and colleagues, including actor Michael Imperioli, remembered him as a loyal friend and a caring individual.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post reports that Pastore celebrated his 80th birthday just weeks before his death, sharing a cake with his “right-hand man,” Stephen Villano. This detail is not included in the other accounts. The BBC and CBS News mention that Pastore was found dead in his Bronx home, while the New York Post specifies that he was found in his City Island home. The New York Post also states that Pastore died of natural causes and was not sick prior to his death, a detail not included in the other accounts. The New York Post attributes the claim about Pastore’s health and cause of death to Stephen Villano, while the other outlets do not mention this.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · CBS News · BBC · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

US representative Marcy Kaptur taken to hospital after car crash

Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) was hospitalized after a car crash in Toledo, Ohio, on Sunday. According to her office, she was a passenger in a vehicle heading to church when the crash occurred. Kaptur, 80, is being treated for non-life-threatening injuries and is described as active and alert. Toledo police responded to a two-vehicle crash shortly before 11 a.m. local time, which they classified as a hit-and-run, also known as a “hit-skip” incident. The crash involved two individuals, including Kaptur, who were transported to a nearby hospital. The investigation is ongoing, with police indicating it is in its early stages.

Kaptur represents Ohio’s 9th Congressional District and is seeking re-election in the fall against Republican Derek Merrin. She is the longest-serving female lawmaker in the history of the U.S. House of Representatives. Her office has expressed gratitude to first responders and constituents for their support following the incident.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Hill both state that Kaptur was a passenger in the vehicle, while The Daily Wire does not specify whether she was driving or a passenger. The Hill and The Washington Examiner mention that the crash occurred around 10:45 a.m., while The Guardian and UPI note it happened shortly before 11 a.m. The Daily Wire and The Hill report that the driver of the vehicle Kaptur was in was identified as Kegan Zimmermann, a detail not included in The Guardian or UPI. The Washington Examiner and The Hill mention that a witness said the driver of the other vehicle fled after being picked up by a third vehicle, a detail not included in The Guardian or The Daily Wire. The Daily Wire does not mention the driver of the vehicle Kaptur was in, while The Hill and The Washington Examiner do.

Sources The Guardian · The Hill · FOX News · The Daily Wire · UPI · Washington Examiner

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

U.S. dollar weakens sharply against the Japanese yen after market interventions

The U.S. dollar weakened sharply against the Japanese yen on Monday after U.S. President Donald Trump and Japan's finance minister confirmed both sides had intervened in markets. Before late last week, the dollar was trading above 163 yen, touching 40-year highs. After regulators were suspected of stepping in, it fell below 160 yen. Early Monday, after the official announcement of the intervention, the dollar dropped about 1% to 156.34 yen. The yen's prolonged weakness against the dollar has been a source of frustration for Tokyo, as Japan imports much of what it consumes, pushing prices higher and increasing inflation. Efforts earlier this year to raise the yen's value against the dollar did little to change the exchange rate.

Japan and the United States confirmed a rare, coordinated yen-buying intervention to halt the Japanese currency’s slide to 40-year lows. The yen leapt after the announcement, gaining as much as 1.4 percent to hit a nearly three-month high of 155.20 per U.S. dollar. The intervention followed a joint statement last year and was aimed at countering excessive volatility and disorderly movements in the Japanese yen. Japan’s Finance Ministry said it would not hesitate to act further if necessary. The move is the first since a 2011 coordinated action to weaken the yen after the earthquake and tsunami in northeastern Japan.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the dollar fell below 160 yen after regulators were suspected of stepping in, while Al Jazeera states the yen gained 1.4 percent to hit a nearly three-month high of 155.20 per U.S. dollar. The Guardian mentions the yen hit its highest level in three months, while BBC notes the yen fell to a 40-year low before the intervention. NPR and Al Jazeera both attribute the intervention to Trump and Japan's finance minister, but NPR includes Trump's comment about Japan's "weakening yen" and the "financial benefit" of the intervention, which Al Jazeera and The Guardian also include. The Guardian and BBC mention the Bank of Japan's June rate hike to 1%, while NPR and Al Jazeera do not. The Guardian and BBC report that Japan may have sold $58.97bn to buy yen, while NPR and Al Jazeera do not specify the amount.

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera · The Guardian · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Corrections

In the edition of Saturday, August 1, 2026, the story “Migrants surge into Spain’s Ceuta enclave, prompting border controls and political backlash”: A pipeline defect caused the 'Where the accounts differ' section to cite outlets as numbered accounts instead of by name. The numbers correspond, in order, to: FOX News (1), Slate (2), New York Post (3), The Daily Wire (4), Washington Examiner (5). The defect is fixed. The original stands unchanged in the archive.

Migrant crisis pushes Italy to restore border checks with Spain, testing Europe's open-border system

Spain faced a massive surge of migrants from Morocco, with over 60,000 crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a single day. The crisis led to the deaths of at least 57 people, many from drowning or being trampled. In response, Italy temporarily restored border controls on travelers arriving from Spain, citing national security concerns. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced the measure would last one month and be coordinated with France to strengthen controls along the Franco-Italian border. The situation has raised questions about the sustainability of the Schengen Area’s open-border policy, as European leaders debate whether migration pressures could lead to a retreat from free movement.

The crisis has also drawn attention from U.S. President Donald Trump, who warned during a Cabinet meeting that a similar situation could unfold in the United States if Democrats win the upcoming midterm elections. Trump criticized Spain’s migration policies, calling them “weak law, bad management,” and linked the events to the Biden administration’s border policies. Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron deployed military forces and drones to strengthen border controls with Spain, citing the need to protect France’s borders.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Spain’s Interior Ministry said 48,300 migrants voluntarily returned to Morocco, leaving fewer than 2,000 in Ceuta, while Straight Arrow News states that Spanish officials estimated about 60,000 entries in 24 hours, a figure briefly posted online before being deleted. The Free Press mentions 60,000 migrants crossing into Ceuta, aligning with Straight Arrow’s estimate. The New York Post claims 60,000 Moroccan immigrants entered Ceuta, while The Daily Wire and BBC also report similar numbers. The New York Post and FOX News both mention the death toll rising to 57, while Straight Arrow News reports 67 deaths. The Daily Wire and BBC note that most migrants returned to Morocco, while FOX News and The Free Press state that the majority of those who entered Ceuta returned to Morocco.

Sources FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · Straight Arrow News · The Free Press · BBC

US stands on the brink of a regional war

The U.S. war with Iran is flaring up across the region, threatening to pull U.S. allies into a fight that Washington and Israel started five months ago. A drone sparked a fire on two gas vessels in the port of Damietta, Egypt, on Wednesday, with no one claiming responsibility. The incident has fueled concerns about a widening war. The U.S. launched retaliatory strikes on Iran for launching missiles on U.S. forces in Jordan earlier this week. Saudi Arabia teamed up with the U.S. on Tuesday night to launch joint strikes on Iranian proxy militias in Iraq, in response to drone strikes on the Saudi Aramco oil processing facility in Abqaiq. Iran pinned the blame for the tanker strike on Israel, while praising Egypt as an “important friend and partner” in the region. Military experts were skeptical of Iran’s ability to keep up such attacks, questioning the strategic prudence of pulling Egypt into the war. Trump during a Cabinet meeting on Friday at Camp David said he was “losing faith” in the country’s ability to make a deal with Iran because “they do lie and they do misrepresent.” The escalations come as Trump faces growing political pressure to end the war.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and Al Jazeera both report that Trump said he would cancel attacks on Iran if a deal is reached, while Associated Press and FOX News describe Trump as saying he would halt attacks pending a deal. The Hill and FOX News mention the drone strike on the Egyptian port of Damietta, while Al Jazeera and Associated Press do not. The Hill attributes the claim that Iran blamed Israel for the tanker strike to Iranian Foreign Minister Abass Araghchi, while Al Jazeera and Associated Press do not attribute the claim. The Hill and Associated Press report that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman raised concerns about U.S. escalating the conflict with Iran, while FOX News and Al Jazeera do not mention this. The Hill and Associated Press report that Trump said he was “losing faith” in the country’s ability to make a deal with Iran, while FOX News and Al Jazeera do not mention this.

Sources The Hill · Associated Press · Newsweek · BBC · FOX News · Al Jazeera

Three people killed and several injured in shooting at In-N-Out in Twin Falls, Idaho: Officials

A shooting occurred at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho, on Saturday afternoon, resulting in three deaths and several injuries. Local authorities confirmed the shooter was among the dead. Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks stated that the threat to the community was over, though the exact number of fatalities and injuries was still under investigation. Multiple people were taken to St. Luke’s Magic Valley Medical Center for treatment. Witnesses described a chaotic scene with people fleeing the area as gunshots rang out.

The incident took place near a busy shopping area, with hundreds of people present at the time. A witness, Lane Koehn, reported seeing a person with an AR-style rifle exit the drive-thru, followed by a man with a pistol firing at the shooter. Another witness, Nayeli Rodriguez, described an older man trying to protect her and her daughters as they fled the restaurant. The In-N-Out restaurant, which opened on July 24, was part of the company’s recent expansion to Idaho.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and CBS News both reported that the shooter was among the dead, while Al Jazeera initially stated the gunman killed two, though later accounts from other outlets corrected this. The Guardian, NPR, and ABC News all reported three deaths, with the Guardian and NPR providing more detail on the victims and the timeline. The Washington Examiner and CBS News mentioned the shooter’s identity was not yet confirmed, while the Guardian and NPR included quotes from witnesses describing the events. The Guardian and NPR also provided more specific details about the victims and the timeline of the shooting, which were not included in the Washington Examiner or CBS News accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera · ABC News · CBS News

Trump administration to dismiss Reflecting Pool charges against David Hearn

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, led by Jeanine Pirro, has moved to drop criminal charges against former Olympic athlete David Hearn, who was accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. In court filings, Pirro acknowledged that the damage to the pool was the result of a botched installation by the contractor, not intentional vandalism. The motion to dismiss was filed after Hearn had pleaded not guilty to one felony count of destruction of property. The administration cited newly provided documents from the Department of the Interior that revealed the damage was due to flawed installation rather than vandalism.

The Reflecting Pool, a historic landmark in Washington, D.C., had undergone a renovation project championed by President Trump. The project, which included resurfacing the pool with “American Flag Blue” paint, was completed before the July 4, 2026, Independence Day celebrations. However, the renovation was plagued by issues such as leaks, algae growth, and peeling sealant. The Department of the Interior initially attributed the damage to vandalism, but later provided evidence showing the problems stemmed from rushed and poorly executed work by the contractor.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Hill both state that Pirro’s office received additional documents from the Department of the Interior after the indictment was returned, which revealed the damage was due to flawed installation. The Hill adds that the National Park Service observed Hearn “violently” tug at the lining before being asked to stop, while UPI and Washington Examiner note that Hearn was accused of tearing the lining but the peeling had already begun before the incident. The Hill and Washington Examiner also mention that the pool was drained for repairs after the July 4 celebrations, a detail not included in Al Jazeera or UPI. The New York Post and Washington Examiner both cite the contractor as Atlantic Industrial Coatings, while The Hill and BBC refer to the contractor as a Virginia-based company.

Sources Al Jazeera · New York Post · The Hill · BBC · UPI · Washington Examiner

Pima County Sheriff Releases Ransom Notes in Nancy Guthrie Investigation

The Pima County Sheriff’s Office released two ransom notes in the ongoing investigation into the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie, an 84-year-old grandmother and mother of NBC’s Savannah Guthrie. The notes, sent to local TV station KOLD and the Guthrie family, describe details of her home and include threats of harm if ransom demands are not met. The sheriff’s office stated the notes contain distinctive linguistic patterns that may help identify the writer. The first note, dated February 2, demanded $4 million in Bitcoin, with a deadline of February 9, and warned of lethal consequences if payment was not received. The second note, sent on February 6, claimed Nancy Guthrie had died shortly after being abducted, attributing her death to heart-related issues. Authorities have not confirmed her death, and the investigation remains active. Savannah Guthrie has publicly appealed for her mother’s return, urging the public to help locate her.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Washington Examiner both mention the first note included a white Apple Watch near Nancy Guthrie’s bed, while the BBC and Straight Arrow News describe it as a white smart watch. The Daily Wire and Washington Examiner also include a specific mention of a damaged flood light, which is not present in the BBC or Straight Arrow News accounts. The Straight Arrow News and Washington Examiner report that the second note was sent on February 6, while the BBC and Washington Examiner also note the second note was sent to the Guthrie family. The Daily Wire and Washington Examiner describe the second note as claiming Nancy Guthrie had died, while the BBC and Straight Arrow News include the same claim. The FOX News account does not mention the release of the ransom notes, focusing instead on video evidence and the sheriff’s confidence in the investigation.

Sources The Daily Wire · CBS News · BBC · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · FOX News

Black Pastor Who Endorsed Abdul El-Sayed Got Paid Big

Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Senate candidate, received payments totaling $75,000 from the Ecumenical Ministers Alliance, a nonprofit linked to Pastor Horace Sheffield III, who endorsed El-Sayed on his radio show. The payments were listed as “political consulting” and made between October 21 and June 1. Sheffield, who is also the father of Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield, has publicly supported El-Sayed without disclosing the payments. In a June 20 video, Sheffield expressed confidence that El-Sayed would beat his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. The nonprofit itself endorsed El-Sayed last month, and El-Sayed publicly thanked the endorsement. In 2018, Sheffield faced similar scrutiny when his nonprofit received payments from candidates for consulting work, including $750 listed as “endorsement fees.”

In Michigan, the race between El-Sayed and Stevens has become a proxy for broader Democratic debates, including the role of corporate money and support for Israel. AIPAC has spent over $50 million to support Stevens, who is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed has criticized U.S. military aid to the country. The race has also drawn national attention, with El-Sayed leading in several recent polls, including a 19-point lead over Stevens in one poll conducted by Zenith Research.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that Sheffield’s nonprofit received $75,000 in payments listed as “political consulting” between October 21 and June 1, while Al Jazeera and Newsweek do not mention the exact amount or timing of the payments. The Daily Wire also notes that Sheffield’s nonprofit endorsed El-Sayed last month, a detail not included in Al Jazeera or Newsweek. The Washington Examiner and Newsweek both mention the $50 million spent by AIPAC on Stevens, but the Daily Wire does not specify the amount, instead stating that AIPAC has spent millions to support Stevens. The Daily Wire also includes information about Sheffield’s past suspension from WFDF and the payments to his nonprofit from other candidates, which are not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources The Daily Wire · Al Jazeera · NPR · Washington Examiner · Newsweek · Mother Jones

Trump blames Minnesota governor, not Iran, for cyberattacks on state's water systems

President Donald Trump on Friday blamed Minnesota's Democratic governor for cyberattacks on the state's water systems, despite U.S. officials previously indicating they are investigating whether Iran or hackers associated with the country could be behind them. Trump made the comments during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David. Minnesota Governor Tim Walz responded by criticizing Trump's remarks, stating that the president "knows exactly who is responsible for this attack" and that "other states were hit too." Walz also attributed the cyberattacks to federal cuts by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which weakened cybersecurity. Over 30 water systems in Minnesota were targeted in a cyberattack over the weekend, according to Minnesota IT Services (MNIT). The attackers targeted systems to remotely monitor and control equipment, including programmable logic controllers (PLCs). The FBI and Environmental Protection Agency issued a nationwide warning about the cyberattacks, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned that cyber threat actors are targeting PLCs and modifying passwords to "lock out operators" from U.S. water systems.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and Straight Arrow News both report that Trump blamed Minnesota and its governor for the cyberattacks, while FOX News, The Daily Caller, and Al Jazeera also mention Trump's comments. However, ABC News and Straight Arrow News note that federal officials are investigating whether Iran or hackers associated with Iran could be behind the attacks, while FOX News and The Daily Caller report that U.S. and state officials told The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the cyberattack. Al Jazeera and Washington Examiner state that no culprit has been identified, and that the FBI is investigating. ABC News and Straight Arrow News also note that Minnesota officials said there was no indication that any water supply was unsafe to drink, while The Daily Caller and Washington Examiner mention that some localities requested residents to conserve water during the attack.

Sources ABC News · Straight Arrow News · FOX News · The Daily Caller · Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner

No source labeled left covered this story.

Trump's comments reignite Blanche confirmation fight

President Donald Trump has continued to push for the confirmation of Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, despite ongoing opposition from Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.). The dispute centers on the "anti-weaponization" fund, a controversial $1.8 billion settlement from Trump's lawsuit against the IRS. Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since April, and his confirmation has been stalled due to demands from Cornyn and Tillis for written assurances that the fund is permanently dead. Trump has defended the fund, stating he wishes it weren't dead, and has threatened to keep Blanche in his acting role until Cornyn and Tillis leave office in January. The White House has also released a demand for Blanche's confirmation "without delay," backed by endorsements from law enforcement groups and lawmakers.

The fund, which would compensate individuals allegedly harmed by a "weaponized" justice system, has faced criticism for potentially benefiting Trump's allies and Jan. 6 rioters. A federal judge previously blocked the fund, calling the settlement a "bad faith" attempt to settle the IRS lawsuit. Blanche has stated the fund is dead, but Cornyn and Tillis have not accepted this, demanding written confirmation. Trump has also criticized the Senate for delaying the confirmation process, with some lawmakers suggesting the vote may be rescheduled for Tuesday.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and The Guardian both report that Trump said the fund is dead but wished it weren't, while UPI and Straight Arrow News describe Trump as saying the fund is dead but will be revived. The Guardian and The Hill note that Cornyn claimed he never had a problem with the fund until after Trump endorsed his opponent, a claim not made by Axios or UPI. The Hill also states that Fetterman said Trump has "zero leverage" over the lame-duck senators, a detail not included in other accounts. FOX News reports that Cornyn and Tillis blocked Blanche's confirmation despite previously supporting Biden's nominee, Merrick Garland, a claim not made by other outlets.

Sources Axios · UPI · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · The Hill · FOX News

Town Declared ‘Abandoned’ After Every Official Resigns Over Water Crisis, Fraud Scandal

The Town of Hartman, Colorado, was declared abandoned by the state after its last elected officials resigned, leaving the community without a functioning government. Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold made the declaration in response to a resident’s petition seeking state intervention. The petition cited a lack of chlorine in the water for over a month, making it non-potable and smelling bad. Residents have been under a boil-water advisory since February. The town previously received $1 million in grants for water repairs, but the funds were unused due to the absence of authorized officials. The Prowers County Board of County Commissioners will now assume responsibility for the town’s roads and water.

The declaration followed years of political infighting, financial mismanagement, and a deteriorating water system. Former Mayor Catherine Ferenandez described the town’s internal conflicts as a “complete mess” due to family rivalries. Residents accused leaders of obstructing elections and neglecting infrastructure. A physical altercation during a board meeting in January led to the resignation of the remaining three trustees, leaving the town without governance. Hartman has about 30 residents, with over 93% living below the poverty line.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire mentions a resident’s petition that included a quote from the New York Post about the water conditions, while The Guardian cites public documents and a letter from resident Jessie Simmons to the secretary of state’s office. The Daily Wire states the petition was submitted to the New York Post, whereas The Guardian attributes the same information to public documents and Simmons’ letter. The Daily Wire also notes that the town had no board of trustees or town clerk, a detail The Guardian confirms. The Guardian adds that Hartman had a population of fewer than 60 at the 2020 census, while The Daily Wire does not specify a population figure. The Guardian includes a quote from resident Shawna Casey objecting to the abandonment, which The Daily Wire does not mention.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian

No source labeled center or lean-left or lean-right covered this story.
